Sample.evidence_source: ['/page/3/Text/10'] While a few men (N = 3, 17%) actively avoided health services—seeing it as "not too manly" other men (N = 6, 33%), struggling with escalating distress, felt they had "nothing to lose" and actively sought help. For the majority of men (N = 9, 50%), help-seeking practices were triggered through unsolicited encounters with health professionals.

Population.evidence_source: ['/page/3/Text/10'] The theorized life histories indicate that there was no set pattern of help seeking among men who engage in suicidal acts.

Type.evidence_source: ['/page/4/Text/10'] The majority of participants' narratives reported that a person-centered approach to care was viewed as more effective and relevant for managing distress and suicidal feelings.

Area.evidence_source: ['/page/3/Text/11'] Men's help-seeking practices could either be facilitated or blocked by the character of the professional support that was available. Men in this study overwhelmingly rejected services that framed emotional distress and suicidal behavior as mental illness. ['/page/3/Text/11'] In contrast, a "personcentered" approach to care, which focused on the concerns of the men, maintained or promoted help-seeking practices.
